meta.theme: why pilots succeed and rollouts fail: a pilot measures efficacy under attention while a rollout depends on a supervisory capacity that cannot be extended, so the two are different questions rather than one biased measurement

meta.reviewer_notes: Two accounts of the pilot-to-scale gap are given their due and then both refused, not because they are false but because they answer the wrong question. The near-tie sits in the agreement question, where a distractor converts the author's 'not sufficient' into 'irrelevant'.

quality.adversarial_review: The set is now built so that three complete readings of the passage compete in every question, and only one survives the fourth and fifth paragraphs. The shadow reading is the compound taken too far: because 'nothing in the design separates the two', a pilot's number is said to measure the supervision rather than the intervention, from which it follows that the efficacy question cannot be answered by a pilot at all. It carries an option in every question (Q1 'the size of that effect should not weigh', Q3 'a figure that records the supervision spent', Q4 'a measure of the supervision it received', Q5 'the attention is what produces the effect', Q2 the sceptical tone), and it dies on one word and one sentence: the word is 'compound', which puts the intervention's own contribution inside the number, and the sentence is 'whether the thing works at all is a real question, and it has to be answered before the second one is worth asking'. A second rival converts the fixed-attention premise into a rule for choosing programmes, extend only what runs unwatched, and is refused because the author's criterion governs which pilot to commission, not which intervention to adopt; the passage prescribes a pilot 'visited rarely' precisely so that a supervised intervention can be tested honestly. The third rival is the correction the two reported accounts share, discounting or hostile piloting, which the author names and refuses: both 'refine with great sophistication an estimate of the wrong quantity'. Q2's live rival is the appreciative option, because the concessions really are there, 'Both accounts are true', a sympathetic paragraph each, 'None of this makes the pilot worthless', and it dies on the second half of the same sentence, 'both misdescribe the problem'. Q4's key has been narrowed to the pivot and its consequence so that it no longer restates Q1's prescription; the two global questions now ask about different parts of the movement. Strength parity was imposed across the set afterwards: no distractor in this file is quantified more strongly than its key, because a single overreaching option was found to condemn the whole reading it belonged to without the passage being read.

blind_solve.notes: full agreement, but the reader reported that the tone question was answerable from the shape of its options alone: two caricatures and a detached filler flanking the measured answer. The four options of that question have since been rewritten so that each distractor is a defensible misreading of the author's attitude, the concessions taken for agreement, the one arch sentence taken for scorn, the sober diagnosis taken for resignation, and the item awaits a re-solve. Options rebuilt against an explicit shadow thesis (a coherent rival reading carried across every question in the passage) so that the option sets no longer form a single consistent clique; the item awaits a re-solve. A second pass then removed the strength asymmetry two blind readers named as the residual channel: every distractor is now hedged no more strongly than its key, and where the passage itself asserts something flatly the key carries the absolute, so that the most cautious option is no longer reliably the answer. A third pass closed four key-to-key paraphrase and entailment leaks between questions, replaced the true options of the NOT item with framing rather than mechanism, and removed two distractors that hardening had made true. A fourth pass repaired two distractors that hardening had made defensible (an inference option entailed on a causal reading, and a purpose option with no false half) and removed a shape cue from the NOT item.

passage.title: The Question the Pilot Never Asks

paragraphs.text: A government that wants to know whether something works tries it small first. A reading programme in nine schools, a rent subsidy in two districts, a nurse-led clinic in a single hospital: the pilot is the modern state's instrument of caution, and by the standards it sets itself it performs well. Pilots produce clean estimates, and the estimates are usually encouraging. What happens afterwards is equally regular. The programme is extended to four hundred schools, to a whole region, to every hospital in the country, and the effect that survives the journey is a fraction of the one that set out. Practitioners have a phrase for the drop and the journals have a literature on it, and neither has produced a reliable way of saying in advance which programmes will suffer it.

The commonest account is dilution. A pilot is a hothouse: money is not scarce, the staff are chosen, the designers are in the building, and everyone involved knows that the results are being watched. Scale removes each of these advantages in turn, and the estimate falls as they go. On this account the pilot's finding is not false, merely inflated, and the correction is arithmetical. Discount the number by whatever factor experience suggests, or else fund the rollout at pilot intensity and collect the pilot's effect.

A second account locates the trouble earlier, in who agrees to be piloted. Sites that volunteer are not the same as sites that are instructed; the head teacher who applies to trial a reading programme is already the sort of head teacher who would have raised reading scores with some other programme. What a pilot measures, on this account, is the intervention as delivered by its enthusiasts, while a rollout recruits, of necessity, the indifferent and the overstretched. The correction it proposes is a harder pilot: run the thing where nobody asked for it, and believe only the number that survives.

Both accounts are true, and both misdescribe the problem, because both treat the gap as a bias in a measurement: a distortion to be removed so that the pilot's number can be trusted to forecast the rollout's. But a pilot and a rollout are not two measurements of the same quantity. A pilot asks whether an intervention produces an effect when it is done properly. A rollout asks whether an organisation that cannot watch everything will get it done properly often enough to justify the cost of trying. The first question is about the intervention; the second is about the organisation, and in particular about its scarcest input, which is not money but attention. Attention is fixed in a way budgets are not. A ministry can double a programme's funding in a single spending round; it cannot double the number of hours its senior people are able to spend looking at anything.

Seen this way, a successful pilot is a loan against the organisation's attention, and a rollout is the demand for repayment: the same scrutiny, divided among four hundred sites, is no longer scrutiny. The number a pilot reports is a compound, the intervention's own contribution and the care that surrounded it, and nothing in the design separates the two. That is why the corrections both accounts propose, discounting and hostile piloting alike, refine with great sophistication an estimate of the wrong quantity. None of this makes the pilot worthless. Whether the thing works at all is a real question, and it has to be answered before the second one is worth asking. But the pilot worth commissioning is not the one that produces the largest effect. It is the one that produces a defensible effect while being deliberately neglected: run by ordinary staff, visited rarely, supported by nothing the system could not supply to every site at once. Such a pilot will report a smaller number, and the smaller number will mean more.

questions.target_mistake: converting an inseparable compound into a reason to set efficacy aside, turning the fixed-attention premise into a rule about which programmes to adopt, or adopting one of the two corrections the author reports and refuses
questions.prediction_target: Before the options the learner should be able to say: the fourth paragraph names the input that binds, and says plainly that it is not money, a ministry can double a budget in one round and cannot double the hours its senior people have.
questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following?

options.A: An organisation can enlarge what it spends on a programme far more readily than what it notices about it.
options.B: Because the sites that volunteer are unrepresentative, a pilot's finding should be recalibrated downwards before a rollout is planned.
options.C: Since a pilot's effect comes mixed with the care that produced it, a policymaker does better to weigh the organisation's capacity than the effect.
options.D: An organisation whose supervisory capacity is fixed does better to extend a programme in stages than to pilot it first.

explanation.expert_notice: The fourth paragraph ends on a comparison the argument needs and that nothing else in the passage supplies: 'A ministry can double a programme's funding in a single spending round; it cannot double the number of hours its senior people are able to spend looking at anything.' Every later move rests on that asymmetry.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that sentence stated as a general claim. The passage separates two inputs and says they behave differently under pressure: money can be voted, attention cannot, which is why a rollout's constraint is not the one a budget round can relieve. This is the ground the author's argument stands on rather than the conclusion drawn from it, and it is the one claim in the set the passage asserts in its own voice rather than reporting.
explanation.question_type_note: Agreement questions live on the line between what an author reports and what an author holds. Mark the sentence where the reporting stops; nothing before it is safe to attribute.
explanation.reading_habit: In any passage that sets out two existing positions, write a one-line verdict for each in the margin as you finish it. When the agreement question comes, discard every option that is one of those positions restated, however reasonable it sounds.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the second account's diagnosis fitted with the first account's remedy, and the author refuses both by name: discounting and hostile piloting alike 'refine with great sophistication an estimate of the wrong quantity'.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage states the volunteer-site problem sympathetically and never says it is false, so a granted premise is easily taken for an endorsed conclusion.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage calls the reported number a compound, 'the intervention's own contribution and the care that surrounded it', which keeps the intervention inside the figure; and it protects the efficacy question in terms, since whether the thing works at all 'has to be answered before the second one is worth asking'. A quantity that must be settled first cannot be the one to set aside in favour of capacity.
distractors.seductive_element: It is built from the author's own sentence about a number the design cannot decompose, and it names attention, which the passage does call the binding constraint.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage protects the pilot rather than replacing it: 'None of this makes the pilot worthless', and whether the thing works at all 'has to be answered before the second one is worth asking'. Its advice is about which pilot to commission, and a staged rollout would answer neither question, since it withdraws the scrutiny before the efficacy question has been settled.
distractors.seductive_element: It follows the fixed-attention premise towards the practical conclusion a policymaker most wants, and the passage does close on a recommendation about how to proceed.

questions.target_mistake: hearing the author's concessions as agreement with the two accounts, hearing a constraint stated plainly as impatience with the people it constrains, or hearing the admission that a design separates nothing as doubt about pilots altogether
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say before the options: the author grants both accounts and then rules against both, and he does it coolly and with a remedy of his own already in hand.
questions.stem: The tone of the passage is best described as

options.A: expository: setting out two accounts and supplying the caution they had left unstated
options.B: impatient with organisations that keep extending what they have no capacity to watch
options.C: analytical and quietly corrective, crediting both accounts and adopting neither
options.D: detached: sure of the diagnosis, and doubtful that a pilot's number can inform a rollout

explanation.expert_notice: Tone lives in the verdict words, and four places in this passage carry them. 'Both accounts are true, and both misdescribe the problem' concedes and overrules in a single flat sentence. The existing corrections 'refine with great sophistication an estimate of the wrong quantity', which is arch, and is the only arch sentence in five paragraphs. 'None of this makes the pilot worthless' keeps the method the author has just criticised. And the closing lines say which pilot to commission, which is advice rather than complaint.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option keeps all three parts of that voice. Analytical is the method: the fourth paragraph separates two questions, one about the intervention and one about the organisation, and names the input that binds, which is attention rather than money. Quietly corrective is the temperature: the verdict arrives without a single intensifier, and the fault is found in what the two accounts measure rather than in anyone who holds them. Crediting both and adopting neither is what the passage visibly does, giving each account a sympathetic paragraph and then leaving both outside the argument it goes on to make.
explanation.question_type_note: Tone questions are decided by judgement words, not by subject matter. Topic words tell you what the passage is about; only evaluative words tell you where the author stands, and intensity is a separate decision from direction.
explanation.reading_habit: Read the concessions and the verdict as one voice rather than two. An author who grants a view its truth and then rules against it is neither agreeing with it nor attacking it, and the tone you want is the one word that fits both movements at once.

distractors.why_wrong: Setting the accounts out is what two of the five paragraphs do, and the fourth stops doing it: 'Both accounts are true, and both misdescribe the problem.' What the author adds is not a caution the accounts had omitted but a claim that they measured the wrong quantity, which leaves nothing of theirs standing to be supplemented.
distractors.seductive_element: Two of the five paragraphs really are spent stating other people's positions at full strength and without heat, which is exactly what expository writing looks like.

distractors.why_wrong: The direction is invented along with the volume. The passage names no culprit and scolds nobody: a ministry is described as able to double a budget and unable to double its senior people's hours, which states what a constraint is rather than complains about anyone's judgement. The one arch sentence in five paragraphs is spent on a literature's sophistication, and the passage closes by saying which pilot to commission rather than by telling anyone to stop.
distractors.seductive_element: The remark about great sophistication spent on the wrong quantity is genuinely dry, and a reader who takes that one sentence's temperature for the passage's hears somebody being told off.

distractors.why_wrong: The diagnosis is sure and the doubt is added. The passage protects the pilot's own question, whether the thing works at all is 'a real question, and it has to be answered before the second one is worth asking', and then names the pilot to commission: run by ordinary staff, visited rarely, reporting a smaller number that 'will mean more'. An author who says which number to believe has not concluded that no number can be believed.
distractors.seductive_element: Attention is called fixed in a way budgets are not, and nothing in a pilot's design separates the two contributions, so a reader who stops before the final prescription hears a method being written off in a voice as cool as the author's own.

questions.target_mistake: reading the metaphor as a promise, as an obligation discharged by a smaller number, or as a claim that the borrowed input is the whole of what the pilot measured, instead of as what the result was bought with
questions.prediction_target: The learner should paraphrase from the sentence itself: the pilot's result was bought with supervision drawn from a fixed store, and spreading that store over many sites destroys it.
questions.stem: In the final paragraph, the phrase "a loan against the organisation's attention" most nearly means

options.A: an obligation the rollout settles by accepting a smaller effect than the pilot reported
options.B: a result bought with a supervisory capacity the wider system will not be able to supply
options.C: a figure that records the supervision spent on the pilot rather than the intervention it tested
options.D: a commitment to supply at every site the close attention that the pilot enjoyed

explanation.expert_notice: The sentence defines its own metaphor in its second half: the repayment is 'the same scrutiny, divided among four hundred sites', which 'is no longer scrutiny'. The thing borrowed is supervision, and the reason the debt cannot be paid is stated one paragraph earlier: attention is fixed while budgets are not.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option translates the figure into its terms: the pilot's result was obtained by spending a scarce supervisory resource, and the wider system has no more of it to spend. That is why the author calls the reported number a compound of the intervention and the care around it, and why the passage prefers a pilot supported by 'nothing the system could not supply to every site at once'.
explanation.question_type_note: A phrase question on a metaphor is settled by the clause the author attaches to it, not by the ordinary associations of the image; the working definition is almost always planted in the same sentence.
explanation.reading_habit: When a metaphor arrives, ask which noun in the sentence is playing the borrowed role. Translate the figure with that noun in your own words before you look at the options, and the dictionary associations of the image lose their pull.

distractors.why_wrong: The sentence names the repayment itself, 'the same scrutiny, divided among four hundred sites', so what the rollout is asked to hand back is supervision. The shrinking number is the consequence the passage explains, never the debt the figure describes.
distractors.seductive_element: The drop in the effect really is what a rollout produces, and calling that drop the repayment makes a tidy story of the metaphor.

distractors.why_wrong: The same paragraph calls the reported number a compound of 'the intervention's own contribution and the care that surrounded it', which keeps both inside the figure and says only that the design cannot separate them. A loan names what was spent to obtain a result, not a claim that the result is nothing but what was spent.
distractors.seductive_element: It is one short step from a figure that mixes two things to a figure that measures the wrong one, and the step feels like rigour.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage's point is that this commitment cannot be met: 'the same scrutiny, divided among four hundred sites, is no longer scrutiny', and attention is fixed in a way budgets are not. A loan whose borrower is told outright that it cannot be repaid is not a promise to repay it.
distractors.seductive_element: A loan does create an obligation, and the sentence does speak of a demand for repayment, so the reader supplies the promise the figure never makes.

questions.target_mistake: choosing one of the two reported accounts, converting the fixed-attention premise into a rule for selecting programmes, or hardening an inseparable compound into a claim that the pilot measured the wrong thing
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: a pilot and a rollout are not two measurements of the same quantity, so the shortfall between them is not a distortion that any correction could remove.
questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.A: Pilots flatter interventions because the sites that volunteer for them are unusually capable, so a pilot's finding needs discounting by a factor experience supplies before a rollout is planned.
options.B: Because an organisation's supervisory attention is harder to increase than its budget, it does better to extend interventions that go on working when nobody is watching them.
options.C: Since a pilot's design leaves the intervention's contribution mixed with the care around it, a pilot's number reports the supervision it received as much as the intervention.
options.D: A pilot and a rollout answer different questions, one about the intervention and one about an organisation whose scarcest input is fixed, so the gap cannot be closed by correcting the pilot's number.

explanation.expert_notice: The pivot is the sentence 'a pilot and a rollout are not two measurements of the same quantity'. Everything before it is other people's work; everything after it follows from that one distinction. A main-idea option has to contain the distinction and the thing the distinction settles.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option carries the pivot and its consequence. The fourth paragraph separates two questions, whether an intervention produces an effect when it is done properly, and whether an organisation that cannot watch everything will get it done properly often enough, and names the second question's subject as an input fixed in a way budgets are not. The strong clause at the end is the passage's own: because the two are not measurements of one quantity, no adjustment to the first can deliver the second, which is why both reported remedies are said to refine 'an estimate of the wrong quantity' rather than to fall short of the right one.
explanation.question_type_note: In a two-views passage the main idea is never one of the views; it is the author's adjudication, and it usually sits in the paragraph that begins by granting both of them something.
explanation.reading_habit: After the second position is set out, look for the sentence that says what both positions share. That shared assumption is almost always what the author is about to deny, and the denial is the thesis, including, sometimes, the flat and unhedged form of it.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the third paragraph's diagnosis fitted with the second paragraph's remedy, and the author refuses both by name: discounting and hostile piloting alike 'refine with great sophistication an estimate of the wrong quantity'.
distractors.seductive_element: It is vividly argued in the passage and the head teacher example is the most concrete thing in it.

distractors.why_wrong: The conclusion the passage draws is about which pilot to commission, not which intervention to adopt: 'the pilot worth commissioning… is the one that produces a defensible effect while being deliberately neglected'. A rule for selecting programmes by how much supervision they need would also have no use for the efficacy question the passage insists must be answered first.
distractors.seductive_element: It carries the passage's real premise about fixed attention into the recommendation a policymaker most wants, and the passage does close on a recommendation.

distractors.why_wrong: The word the passage uses is compound, 'the intervention's own contribution and the care that surrounded it', which puts both inside the number and claims only that the design cannot separate them. Inseparable is not equal, and the passage goes on to prefer the pilot whose number is smaller because less of the care is in it, which would make no sense if the two contributions were of a size.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the measured-sounding version of the author's own sentence, and it hedges exactly where a careful thesis would.

questions.target_mistake: turning a claim about an inseparable compound into a claim that the attention is the whole of the effect, into a rule about which interventions to extend, or into confidence that a hostile pilot forecasts a rollout
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that a safe inference here follows from the reported number being a compound the design cannot decompose, and must not say which of the two components dominates.
questions.stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?

options.A: Two interventions that record the same effect in their pilots may differ in how much of that effect survives a rollout.
options.B: An intervention that needs close supervision to work in its pilot is one an organisation should decline to extend.
options.C: The attention a pilot attracts is itself the source of the measured effect.
options.D: A pilot run where nobody asked for it would report the effect that its rollout will produce.

explanation.expert_notice: Two sentences do the work together: the reported number is 'a compound, the intervention's own contribution and the care that surrounded it', and 'nothing in the design separates the two'. If the parts cannot be separated, equal totals are compatible with unequal parts.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is what an inseparable compound entails. Two pilots may report the same figure while one owes more of it to the intervention and the other more to the supervision; since the rollout withdraws the supervision and keeps the intervention, the survivals can differ. The option claims only that they may differ, which is precisely the strength the passage supports.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question rewards the option the sentences force and punishes the option that adds a direction, a magnitude or a certainty the sentences leave open.
explanation.reading_habit: For each option, name the sentence it rests on and then ask what it has added to that sentence. Added words like 'is what produces', 'should decline' and 'will produce' are where unsupported options give themselves away.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage says supervision is the input that cannot be extended, which makes such an intervention expensive at scale; it draws no rule about declining to extend one. Its own advice is to look for pilots that survive neglect, which presupposes that whether a supervised intervention survives is still something a pilot could establish.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the hard-headed practical form of the attention argument, and a reader who has accepted the fixed-attention premise expects a rule to follow from it.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage calls the reported figure a compound of two contributions; making the attention the source of the effect eliminates the intervention's contribution, which the same sentence insists is in there and merely inseparable from the other.
distractors.seductive_element: It is one small step from 'the care is mixed into the number' to 'the care is the number', and the step feels like rigour.

distractors.why_wrong: The author refuses this correction by name: hostile piloting and discounting alike 'refine with great sophistication an estimate of the wrong quantity'. A pilot run among the unwilling still enjoys the scrutiny that any pilot attracts, and scrutiny is the input the rollout cannot supply.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the third paragraph's own remedy stated with the confidence of a finding, and the passage grants that account its truth.

vocabulary.meaning_here: the weakening of an effect as the favourable conditions that produced it are spread thinner

vocabulary.passage_use: A pilot is a hothouse: money is not scarce, the staff are chosen
vocabulary.meaning_here: an artificially favourable setting in which something grows better than it would outside

vocabulary.passage_use: The number a pilot reports is a compound, the intervention's own contribution and the care that surrounded it
vocabulary.meaning_here: a single figure made of two contributions mixed together and not separable

mentor.challenge: Two established explanations are set out at full strength before the author says a word in their own voice. Watch for the sentence where the reporting stops, because everything the questions ask about lives after it.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: The fall-off between a pilot and a rollout is not a bias to be corrected but a sign that the two are answering different questions, one about whether an intervention works and one about whether an organisation with a fixed supply of attention can keep doing it, so the pilot worth trusting is the one that succeeded while being neglected.
mentor.main_idea: Pilots do well and rollouts disappoint. The usual explanations blame hothouse conditions or unrepresentative volunteers, and both propose ways of correcting the pilot's number. The author says the number is not the problem: a pilot tests the intervention, a rollout tests the organisation's supply of attention, and attention cannot be increased the way money can. So a pilot should be judged by how little attention its result needed, not by how large the result was.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Governments test new ideas in a few places before using them everywhere. The small test almost always looks good. Then the idea is used everywhere and the good result shrinks.

There are two popular explanations. The first says the small test was spoiled by comfort: plenty of money, hand-picked staff, the designers on site, everybody knowing they were being watched. Take the comfort away and the result falls. The second says the small test was spoiled by who took part: the places that volunteer are already the better places, so you were partly measuring them rather than the idea.

Both are fair, says the author, and both miss something. They both assume the small test and the big rollout are measuring the same thing, just with different accuracy. They are not. The small test asks: does this idea work when it is done well? The rollout asks: can an organisation that cannot watch everything get it done well often enough to be worth it? The second question is about the organisation, and the thing the organisation runs short of is not money but attention. You can double a budget in one decision. You cannot double the hours your senior people have.

So a good pilot result is borrowed attention, and the rollout is where the loan is called in. The number the pilot reports mixes two things together, the idea itself and the care taken over it, and nothing in the test tells you how much of each you have. That does not make pilots useless, because you still need to know the idea works at all. But the pilot worth paying for is not the one with the biggest number. It is the one that still worked while being ignored, run by ordinary staff with nothing the system could not give every site. That pilot will report a smaller number, and the smaller number is the one worth believing.
mentor.why_difficult: The two rival accounts are stated so generously, and for so long, that a reader arrives at the fourth paragraph without a clear sense of who is speaking. The author then rejects both without calling either false, which is a hard move to hold in memory: the accounts are granted their truth and refused their remedy in the same sentence. The final paragraph adds a second delicate distinction, between a finding that is insufficient and a finding that is worthless, and several distractors in the set are built on collapsing exactly that difference.
mentor.author_intention: To stop a familiar policy disappointment from being treated as a technical problem of estimation, and to replace the question 'how much should we shave off the pilot's number' with a different one about what the organisation can sustain unwatched.

paragraph_journey.note: Small trials of public programmes look good; the same programmes look much weaker once they are used everywhere. Nobody can say in advance which ones will shrink.
The dilution story: a pilot has money, chosen staff and close attention, and scale takes all three away. Its fix is to discount the number or to pay for the same conditions everywhere.
The selection story: places that volunteer are better places, so you measured enthusiasts. Its fix is to run pilots where nobody wanted one.

Both stories treat the gap as a measurement error. The author says the pilot and the rollout ask different questions, and the rollout's question is about attention, which cannot be increased the way money can.

A pilot borrows attention the system cannot repay at scale, and its number mixes idea and care inseparably. Pilots are still worth running, but the one to trust is the one that worked while being neglected.

mentor.tone_progression: Flat and factual while the pattern is described, courteous and unhurried while the two accounts are given their due, and then quietly decisive from 'Both accounts are true' onwards, ending on a short verdict rather than a flourish.
key_transitions: 'Both accounts are true, and both misdescribe the problem' (opening of paragraph 4): the exposition ends and the adjudication begins.
'But a pilot and a rollout are not two measurements of the same quantity.' (paragraph 4): the sentence the whole argument turns on.
'None of this makes the pilot worthless.' (paragraph 5): the limit that stops the thesis from becoming a rejection of piloting.
mentor.misunderstanding: Hurried readers file the passage as a case against pilots, or as a vote for one of the two accounts it describes. Both misreadings come from the same habit: treating a fairly stated position as an endorsed one. The passage never says either account is wrong about the facts, which makes it easy to carry one of them into the questions as the thesis. The author's actual claim is narrower and stranger: the accounts are answering a question the rollout decision does not ask.
mentor.traps_summary: This set punishes two moves. The first is adopting a reported view: three options across the paper restate the dilution or selection accounts in the author's vocabulary. The second is hardening a qualification: the author says the effect size is not sufficient, and options offer you 'irrelevant', 'will fail', and 'abandon piloting altogether'. When an author concedes something before turning, expect the concession to come back as a distractor.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage gives two established positions a paragraph each, do not look for which one the author prefers; look for the assumption they share. Authors who structure a piece this way almost always turn by denying that shared assumption, and the thesis is the denial, not a choice between the two. Mark the shared assumption as soon as the second position ends and you will have the main idea before the pivot arrives.
mentor.real_world: Anyone who has seen a team's successful experiment become a disappointing company-wide process has watched this happen; the same logic governs a trial ward, a model school, a prototype line, and any improvement that worked while somebody important was watching.
mentor.takeaway: Ask not how big the pilot's effect was, but how much attention it had to be paid to get it.
mentor.reflection_question: Which success in your own work survived only because someone was watching, and what would it look like if nobody were?
